Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter’s leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning depends on the receiver, target behavior, and how the required corrections are represented in the learned update.

Fine-tuning changes the behavior of a pretrained model by writing an update relative to what that model already knows. How many bits are actually required to preserve this acquired behavior? Parameter count, adapter rank, and numerical precision measure storage, but need not measure the information that matters functionally. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) provides a clean setting for studying this question: the base model remains frozen while the learned update is isolated in a separate adapter that can be compressed after training. We take a receiver-relative rate–distortion view of this process. As illustrated in Figure 1 , fine-tuning acts as an encoder, the adapter as a finite-rate message, and the frozen model as side information available when that message is decoded. We measure rate by the exact serialized size of a compressed adapter and distortion by the behavior of the resulting composed model. For a fixed retention target, the behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} is the smallest measured rate that preserves the required fraction of the held-out fine-tuning gain. This operational definition exposes a gap between numerical and behavioral compression. Lower weight reconstruction error need not preserve more learned behavior, and comparable bit budgets can have different effects depending on where compression acts. Behavioral rate also increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budget. Most importantly, the same datasets can require substantially different rates across frozen models, with their ordering changing across receivers. A correction-gradient spectrum computed from the data and receiver ranks R ⋆ R^{\star} well within a fixed receiver, but does not transfer reliably across new receivers. ction-gradient spectrum computed from the data and receiver ranks R ⋆ R^{\star} well within a fixed receiver, but does not transfer reliably across new receivers. Compression can also reveal structure within a learned update. Under deliberately corrupted reasoning supervision, fine-tuning can strongly damage the frozen model, yet aggressive compression recovers much of the lost performance and can exceed the frozen baseline. On Qwen2.5-7B, for example, GSM8K accuracy falls from 77.6% to 23.7% after corrupted fine-tuning and returns to 82.9% after compression. Singular-direction analyses show that harmful and useful effects are distributed unevenly across the update, while matched-norm controls show that the recovery is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. Finally, once an update has been trained, its behavioral rate closely tracks how far it can be shrunk before losing its gain. A simple codec-specific rule, R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) ≈ α 90 / γ R^{\star}(0.90)\approx\alpha_{90}/\gamma , achieves an RMSE of 0.068 bits per value on 42 checkpoints from five receivers not used to fix the rule, although the evaluation remains retrospective. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning is not an intrinsic property of the data or of parameter displacement alone: it depends on the frozen receiver, the behavior to preserve, and how the learned corrections are represented within the update.

Estimating α 90 \alpha_{90} requires evaluating only five scales of the uncompressed update on 64 held-out examples, while γ \gamma is obtained from the adapter weights; no regression coefficient is fitted. After fixing the rule on six adapters from two receivers, Figure 7 (b) compares this estimate with measured rates on 42 checkpoints from five other receivers. It achieves an RMSE of 0.068 bits per value ( R 2 = 0.95 R^{2}=0.95 ). On a broader archive of 58 adapters spanning 34 corpora, the RMSE is 0.105 bits per value. Additional baselines, disjoint-evaluation controls, and trained-update predictors are reported in Appendix C.4 . These experiments remain retrospective: although the rule was fixed independently of the reported receiver panels, their behavioral rates had already been measured when it was formulated. We therefore interpret Equation 7 as a retrospective empirical approximation rather than a prospectively validated prediction law. The same response curve connects the two main empirical findings of the paper. In Section 5 , moving back along the learned update can remove harmful behavior and recover performance; here, the distance one can move before losing useful behavior closely tracks the rate required to preserve the fine-tune. (b) α 90 / γ \alpha_{90}/\gamma against measured R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) for 42 checkpoints on five receivers not used to fix the rule (blue) and 58 archived adapters spanning 34 corpora (grey). Our experiments show that behavioral rate is receiver-relative: the same dataset can require different rates across frozen models, while parameter-space reconstruction error alone does not predict which compressed updates preserve behavior. At the same time, the success of the shrinkability approximation indicates that, once an update has been learned, much of its compression difficulty can be summarized by the behavioral response obtained when moving back along that update. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, R ⋆ R^{\star} is an operational, codec-dependent rate rather than an information-theoretic optimum; different adapter parameterizations or codecs may induce different measured rates. Second, the correction-spectrum statistic is only a proxy for the full receiver-relative geometry and does not transfer reliably across receivers. Third, the shrinkability rule is supported by broad but retrospective evaluation, and remains to be validated prospectively on rates not observed when the rule is formulated. Finally, our recovery experiments use deliberately corrupted supervision to create a controlled mixture of useful and harmful effects. Whether the same structure governs naturally occurring fine-tuning errors remains an open question.

2610.10965:3b9757172ea184b4a5698b6853808.question: In the NanoGPT speedruns, how do the thresholded Muon variants compare with standard Muon and normalized SGD on validation loss, training time, and effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices? What controls and limitations qualify the conclusions about small versus large singular directions?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. In this paper, we will explore a method to target this orthogonalization to singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ \tau , and we will also experiment with different values for this threshold, thus allowing us to interpolate between SGD and Muon with a spectrally targeted version. Specifically, we will apply these Muon variants to the two speedrun tasks originally used to show Muon’s performance, the CIFAR-10 dataset with a convolutional network, and the NanoGPT large language model, just as in Jordan et al. (2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices. This allows us to explore what characteristics of matrix optimizers lead to richer learning.

Figure 3 (a) shows that the singular values are spread across many orders of magnitude, indicating that gradient matrices in the language model setting are very poorly conditioned. This variation does not stem from variation between different matrices: as we can see in Figure 4 (a), the effective rank of the gradient stays below about 280 for most of training. This implies a low-entropy and highly nonuniform distribution within each matrix. Figure 3 (a) also displays the distribution of the gradients after Nesterov momentum is applied. Momentum thins out the low end of the spectrum, suggesting that it suppresses some noisy directions, but otherwise leaves its shape alone and simply shifts scale. This distribution was used to select the absolute thresholds τ \tau for targeted Muon. Averaged over matrices, the top arm lifts about 1% to 28% of the singular directions, and the bottom arm lifts from nearly all of the directions down to about 30%. In terms of squared Frobenius norm, the lifted band holds 32–96% of the momentum in the top arm and at most 13% in the bottom arm. Note that τ \tau is absolute while the bulk of the spectrum sits at different levels in different matrices, so the same τ \tau lifts very different fractions of different matrices. In the top arm this compounds: a matrix whose spectrum falls below τ \tau only gets its raw momentum and effectively stops training, so at the larger thresholds most of the deeper layers are left untouched. Also note that every momentum singular value is far below one, so the targeted region is always amplified, not suppressed.

Validation loss was monitored throughout and remained almost exactly at training loss, so overfitting is not a concern. Every Muon variant drops the loss faster than AdamW over the first hundred steps (Figure 3 (b)), and the lead grows with how much of the spectrum is lifted. Lifting only the top few directions with a high τ \tau already gets much of Muon’s early advantage, but the lead reverses within a few hundred steps, and every top dose ends up behind AdamW with warmup, the smallest ones even behind NSGD (Table 1 ). This is not a matter of step size. Raising the learning rate of the top variants only makes them worse and collapses their rank further (Figure 5 (c)), while Muon at a tenth of its learning rate loses just 0.05. Figure 3 (c,d) plots the final loss against τ \tau and against the fraction of the momentum that is orthogonalized. For both top and bottom targeting, loss falls monotonically with the portion of directions orthogonalized. However, the two arms are not symmetric. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix gets within 0.03 of Muon while orthogonalizing only about 13% of the momentum matrix’s magnitude, while lifting only the top directions remains well short even when they make up 96% of it, and the smallest top doses do worse than lifting nothing. This answers one part of our original question. Despite being a very small portion of the momentum magnitude, the small singular values are not noise. The model can be usefully trained on them, but only once they are amplified to full scale. (a) Gradient effective rank (b) Update effective rank (c) Value matrix effective rank (d) Output matrix effective rank (e) MLP effective rank

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (a) Tangent alignment (b) Spectrum-changing update by singular direction (c) Final loss vs. parameter rank

Figure 5: How much of the update changes the spectrum, and where. (a) Log-barrier of the isospectral tangent fraction, averaged over matrices; the grey dotted line is the value for a random rotation, the orange dotted line marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and dashed lines are the warmup variants. (b) Share of the spectrum-changing part of the update at each singular direction of the parameter, ranked by singular value, averaged over matrices and steps 100–1500; the dotted line is uniform. (c) Final validation loss against final parameter effective rank, including the learning rate controls; the bottom-targeted runs at τ ≤ 4 × 10 − 4 \tau\leq 4\times 10^{-4} leave their MLP output matrices barely trained. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

2610.22438:f1cba59efe95e2bd1c2fd70038c9f.question: Across the 13 released language-model fine-tuning pairs, how do stable rank and energy-coverage rank compare with shape-matched random updates, pretrained weights, and matched fine-tunes without alignment content? What controlled results support the conclusions, and what limitations affect their interpretation?

passages.text: Studies of what fine-tuning does to a language model often summarise the weight update Δ ​ W \Delta W by its rank. We compare the rank measures used for this against the same measures on a random matrix of the same shape, and against two harder references: the pretrained weights, and matched fine-tunes without alignment content. Measures that count directions put our fine-tuning updates only a little below noise; stable rank, computed from the same singular values, puts them far below. Both are right: an update has a few strong directions on top of a long tail. The pattern holds for thirteen released pairs up to 8B parameters, and it is not a mark of alignment: with training held fixed, instruction data does not stand out from Wikipedia or code, DPO gives the same update whether its preference labels are real or half swapped at random (one model, modest preference strength), and scrambled text gives the most concentrated update of all. Applied to a recent claim that post-training is superficial because the effective rank of the weights barely changes, the baselines show that a random update of the same size leaves that rank almost unchanged while wrecking the model, and that an edit built on the effective rank of the update has no measurable effect in our tests. Rank measures of weight updates need a noise baseline, and claims about alignment need a control without alignment content.

A value of any of these measures only means something next to its value for a matrix with no structure. For our own runs the baseline is the difference between two independent random initialisations of the same model; for released models, one Gaussian draw for each matrix, with the same shape. The spectrum of such a matrix follows the Marchenko–Pastur law, whose upper edge (the Bai–Yin limit, Bai and Silverstein, 2010 ) gives a stable rank close to m ​ n ( m + n ) 2 , \frac{mn}{(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n})^{2}}, a quarter of r r for square matrices. Our random-init pairs match this to within 0.01 for every matrix shape of Qwen2.5-0.5B (Table 10 in Appendix B ), and the two baselines agree: on Qwen2.5-0.5B the stable rank is 0.436 for the random-init pair and 0.434 for the Gaussian matrices. Beating this baseline is necessary but not sufficient. A Gaussian matrix is the least structured baseline possible, and any difference between two trained matrices beats it: the pretrained weights W W themselves have a stable rank well below noise, and so does the difference between two unrelated trained checkpoints (§ 3 ). The noise value tells the reader how to read a number; it does not by itself show that an update is special. So we use two further references: the pretrained weights W W , and fine-tunes on data with no alignment content, trained the same way (§ 4.3 ).

Released instruct models go through much larger and more varied post-training than our runs. The same pattern holds for all thirteen pairs (Figure 3 , Table 3 ). The threshold count reads 91–99%, close to noise; stable rank puts every update 1.6 to 27 times below noise, and dropping the top direction changes little, so no single outlier drives it. Every update also has tens to hundreds of directions above the largest singular value a same-size Gaussian matrix would have (Table 13 ). For most pairs, bf16 rounding is not a concern: 91–100% of their directions are stronger than anything rounding alone can produce. For three it is: 14% of the entries of the Qwen2.5-1.5B update, and 39% and 52% of the OLMo DPO and RL updates, are exactly zero, and only 78%, 13% and 3% of their directions rise above the simulated rounding floor (Tables 3 and 13 ). For these updates much of what the threshold count counts may be rounding. Rounding adds many tiny singular values, which stable rank largely ignores. The OLMo 2 stages show where post-training changes the weights. Almost all of the change is in SFT: its update is 9.8% of the size of the weights, has stable rank 0.080 against 0.336 for noise, and the whole base-to-instruct update has the same size and shape to within 0.001. The DPO and RL stages are tiny, under half a percent of the weights, and only 13% and 3% of their directions rise above the simulated rounding floor. Their very low stable rank therefore reflects a few real directions on top of rounding, and we draw no conclusion about preference training from them; our own DPO runs (§ 4.3 ) are the controlled test.

• One model for preference training. The DPO runs and their swapped control are on Qwen2.5-0.5B only. Reinforcement learning appears only in the released OLMo 2 stage, which is too small to measure above rounding. • Scale of our own training. Our fine-tunes are 0.36B and 0.5B parameters with about two million tokens per epoch. The measurement results hold on released models up to 8B, but we do not study training at that scale. • Tokens or steps. Matching the training tokens leaves the code runs with 2.6–2.7 times fewer optimizer steps than SFT; matching the steps gives them 2.5–2.7 times more tokens. No single control matches both, and the two give different code updates. • Which null. A Gaussian matrix is the least structured baseline possible, and even the difference of two unrelated trained checkpoints beats it. We add the pretrained weights as a harder reference, and matched fine-tunes without alignment content as the real test, but other baselines (for instance updates from other optimizers) could tell more. • Seeds. The SFT, wikitext, code and DPO runs were repeated once; the shuffled-words and step-matched runs were not. Two seeds bound the run-to-run variation only roughly. • Released models are black boxes. Apart from OLMo 2, their data and recipes differ in many ways at once, so they test the measurement, not any claim about alignment. • Loss masking differs. SFT computes the loss on answer tokens only, the controls on every token; the tokens seen are matched, the tokens trained on are not. • The shuffled-words result is unexplained. The one explanation we tested, alignment with token frequency, is shared by other runs.

• Directions, measured coarsely. The overlap of top-16 subspaces shows that the data steers the directions of an update; it does not say which directions, or what they do. • The edit experiment is narrow: one model, non-thinking mode only, and 198 GPQA questions, which leaves intervals of about ± 3 \pm 3 points. • One random-update test. The damage test uses one model, Qwen3-0.6B, and one task, GSM8K.

Rank measures that count directions describe fine-tuning updates as nearly full rank and put them only a little below random matrices of the same shape. Measures that weigh the top directions show the same updates to be far more concentrated than noise, and more concentrated than the pretrained weights. Both are right: the updates have a few strong directions and a long tail that holds most of the energy. With the amount of training held fixed, the data shapes an update somewhat, but instruction tuning does not stand out from Wikipedia or code; DPO gives the same shape and directions with real or half-swapped preferences; and scrambled text gives the most concentrated update. The shape is a property of fine-tuning, not a mark of alignment. An unchanged effective rank of the weights after post-training is what a random update of the same size also produces, and an edit built on the effective rank of the update does nothing measurable on two benchmarks. draft.reason: The screened papers cover the core research directions with inspected evidence. Remaining uncertainty that could change the selection includes unverified implementation reproducibility and whether results from smaller models, simplified theory, or separate systems benchmarks transfer to larger-scale pretraining.

selections.summary: Spectral weight decay applies additive singular-value shrinkage. In LLaMA models up to 500M parameters, it improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss; at 500M and a 4% distortion budget, the reported compression is 1.89× versus 1.14× after standard weight decay.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses whether training can make weights easier to compress without losing model quality.

evidence.quote: For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay.

selections.summary: Ori tracks drifting low-rank gradient subspaces during LLM pretraining. At rank 16 on a 130M model, it reports validation perplexity of 43.61 versus 60.29 for GaLore and 54.05 for OSD. Its reported memory figures measure the optimizer step, not total peak training memory.
selections.relevance: Direct comparison for low-rank-gradient pretraining under tight rank and memory constraints.

evidence.quote: when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05).
Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step.

selections.summary: Monarch–Muon combines structured weights with matrix-aware optimization. Quality runs favor it over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure; separate 6.89B systems measurements report 52.94 versus 68.87 GB peak memory against dense Muon. The quality and largest-scale systems results are not from the same run.
selections.relevance: Useful for assessing quality, memory, and speed tradeoffs as model width increases.

evidence.quote: Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model
The systems experiments measure training operations on larger reference architectures, separately from the complete quality runs in Appendix A.1 .

selections.summary: A module-matched LoRA rank sweep studies label noise across vision models and Qwen2.5-7B. In the 7B experiment, every sampled rank, including parameter parity, remains behind dense fine-tuning on test NLL across three paired seeds.
selections.relevance: Direct evidence on LoRA rank, memorization, and generalization under noisy labels.

evidence.quote: Every sampled rank, parity included, remains behind dense in all three seeds
Seeds control the subset, the noise draw, the head init and the adapter init, and are shared across arms, so the differences below are paired.

selections.summary: An SVD-free Rényi-2 regularizer encourages LoRA updates to use more of their configured rank. Across mixed-domain sweeps on three models, λ=0.01 reduces mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16, though the paper reports configuration-dependent learning–retention tradeoffs.
selections.relevance: Connects effective rank and spectral regularization to practical language-model fine-tuning.

evidence.quote: In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA
the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off.

selections.summary: Derives how GD, SignGD, ideal Muon, Shampoo, and a K-FAC model change singular-mode birth, persistence, and decay in deep matrix factorization. The phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, so they are not direct LLM performance claims.
selections.relevance: Provides a theoretical framework for how optimizer geometry changes spectra and low-rank bias.

evidence.quote: Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC.

selections.summary: BMuon changes Muon’s geometry to favor structured MLP-channel compressibility. In a three-seed 1B LLaMA-style experiment, it better withstands post-training pruning, but unpruned perplexity is worse than Muon’s: 12.84 versus 10.92.
selections.relevance: A particularly informative counterpoint on compressibility versus uncompressed model quality.

evidence.quote: On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning.
Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

selections.summary: CORE is a training-free research-agent harness that retrieves passages but returns selected snippets, with source expansion and deduplication. Its closed-search comparisons report higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than two harness baselines across three agent models and benchmarks.
selections.relevance: Directly informs retrieval and context-management design for a handwritten research-digest harness.

evidence.quote: CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level.
Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison

selections.summary: Idea2Prior records candidate identities, filtering reasons, evidence availability, and final rankings for idea-to-paper search. Its historical 30-query comparison reports 16/30 target hits, but includes replacement runs and does not establish a contamination-free evaluation.
selections.relevance: Relevant to auditable paper retrieval and ranking, with evaluation caveats important for digest-agent design.

evidence.quote: The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research.
This historical record does not establish a newly controlled, contamination-free evaluation.

selections.summary: Analyzes when frozen-backbone fine-tuning objectives admit low-rank solutions. Trace-norm regularization yields global minimizers whose rank is controlled by a finite-rank observation map; a separate factorized-LoRA result requires a generic positive-semidefinite perturbation.
selections.relevance: Connects nuclear-norm regularization and LoRA rank to the geometry of observed features.

evidence.quote: This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size.
after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank.

limitations: Selections are limited to the supplied screened corpus; unseen papers may be stronger matches.
Code availability and reproducibility were not verified.

Several findings come from simplified theory, smaller models, or benchmarks separate from the largest systems measurements; they should not be generalized to large-scale LLM pretraining without further testing.

candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. candidates.title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
